description: A named agent explicitly described as being of the jinn who defies the command in the Adam account.

being_types.note: Partial comparative mapping only. Qur'an 18:50 identifies Iblis as of the jinn; it does not license treating all jinn as demonic, wish-granting, or morally identical.

narrative_archetypes.note: Descriptive of the cited narrative action only; no generic 'devil' or demonology equivalence is asserted.

canon_status: Primary sacred-text witness; theological narrative record

supports: Iblis refuses when the angels are commanded to prostrate before Adam.
Iblis is described as being of the jinn and as defying his Lord's command.

comparison_cautions: This is a record of a Qur'anic sacred narrative, not a generic fantasy villain template.
The source term jinn has diverse theological and cultural treatment; Iblis's narrative role must not be generalized to all jinn.
Later folklore, tafsir, hadith, and literary depictions are not evidence for this record.

description: The named human participant in the selected Iblis narrative: Iblis refuses the command concerning him.

being_types.note: A limited comparative mapping for the human participant in this narrative; it does not reduce sacred anthropology to a fantasy ancestry category.

canon_status: Primary sacred-text witness; included only as the named counterparty in the Iblis passage

supports: Adam is named as the figure before whom Iblis refuses the commanded prostration.

comparison_cautions: Adam is included solely to retain a character-only, cited relationship within the selected Qur'anic narrative.
This sacred-text record is not a statement that Adam is a generic fantasy human archetype.
No extra-Qur'anic genealogy, theology, or adaptation is asserted.

description: A named figure for whom jinn work by his Lord's permission in the selected Qur'anic account.

being_types.note: Limited comparative mapping only; the witness does not present a player-style ancestry classification.

metaphysical_laws_and_rituals.note: The cited wording grounds the action in divine permission; it is not evidence for a transferable binding ritual or magic system.

canon_status: Primary sacred-text witness; theological narrative record

supports: Jinn work before Sulayman by his Lord's permission.
The cited passage continues the account of the jinn's work for Sulayman.
The passage states that the jinn did not know the unseen.

comparison_cautions: The passage attributes this relationship to divine permission; it must not be recast as an ordinary technique for controlling spirits.
No seal, ring, grimoire, wish, or later folkloric ability is included because it is absent from this bounded witness.
The record does not collapse Qur'anic theology, later tafsir, regional lore, or The Thousand and One Nights into one continuity.
